title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a credible-seeming interview between two real, named public figures, promoting an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure is not inside a legitimate AI deployment gone wrong, but in the deliberate misuse of AI tools to produce disinformation at scale. The fabricated interview was embedded within a broader constructed environment of fake brands, articles, reviews, and advertisements, meaning no single piece of content was the whole deception.

What makes this pattern notable is the layered credibility it builds. Earlier investment scams relied on a single fake image or post, which could be identified and removed more easily. Here the infrastructure of apparent legitimacy, multiple fake assets reinforcing one another, raises the cost of detection for ordinary consumers and requires regulators to identify and remove many connected pieces rather than one.

What is not established is who produced the content, whether any specific AI product or platform was used to generate it, or whether any legal finding has been made against any party. The figures ASIC reports, including the 182 percent rise in scams removed and the surges in phishing and fake investment platforms, describe a trend the regulator has observed, not a proven causal link between any particular technology and those outcomes.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fabricated article recently circulated online featuring a fake interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never occurred, but the scam represents a growing trend of AI-generated investment schemes. ASIC reports that such sophisticated frauds are becoming increasingly common, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams surged 279 percent, while fake investment platforms jumped 151 percent.

Scammers increasingly impersonate high-profile Australians, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart among the most commonly targeted. Rather than using single fake images, criminals now construct elaborate webs of deception involving fake brands, news articles, reviews, and advertisements to build credibility. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers and independently check them through official registers before investing. Kohler argues that platforms hosting such content should face heavy penalties.
